strengths: Novel asymmetric perturbation insight providing an interesting alternative to symmetric perturbation, with clear motivation via impossibility result (Theorem 3.1)
Rigorous theoretical analysis with complete proofs; Theorem 3.3's near-linear behavior insight is elegant and well-reasoned
Provides O(1/t) last-iterate convergence guarantee without requiring decaying perturbations or careful parameter scheduling
Comprehensive treatment spanning theory, algorithms (AsymP-GDA, AsymP-CFR+), and experiments across multiple game classes
Good reproducibility with provided code, detailed experimental settings, and complete proofs in appendix
weaknesses: Restricted theoretical scope: Theorems 3.3 and 4.1 apply only to bilinear games; extensive-form experiments use behavioral form with no theoretical guarantees, creating a significant theory-practice gap

Overstated claims about parameter tuning: Requires μ ∈ (0, α/max||x*||) where α depends on X* and is unknown; in pathological cases (Remark 4.3), α→0 rendering the bound vacuous; claims of avoiding fine-tuning are not well-supported

Limited practical significance of impossibility result: Theorem 3.1 shows exact equilibrium not recovered for μ not in a measure-zero set, but doesn't explain why O(μ) approximation error is unacceptable compared to alternatives; exceptional parameter values are artificial constructs

Weak experimental validation: Small problem instances (3×3 to 5×5 matrices); missing comparisons to optimistic methods (OGDA, extragradient) in extensive-form games; arbitrary μ selection (0.01, 1) without principled guidance; improvements shown but not quantified precisely; no wall-clock time comparisons

Incremental algorithmic novelty: AsymP-GDA and AsymP-CFR+ are straightforward modifications (perturb one player); proofs rely heavily on existing techniques (Wei et al. 2021); main innovation is asymmetry observation itself

Uncharacterized constants and missing practical guidance: Theorem 4.1 involves unknown constants β and σ; no procedure provided for practitioners to determine suitable μ for new problems; Remark 4.3's anchoring workaround requires knowing α

Incomplete analysis: No computational complexity comparison; robustness to approximate gradients/noise not addressed; dimension-dependence not characterized; behavioral-form extensive-form games analyzed only empirically without theoretical justification

Practical algorithm (AsymP-GDA) with O(1/t) last-iterate convergence guarantee, addressing cycling issues of unperturbed GDA
Comprehensive experiments across multiple game types with error bars over 100 seeds and detailed reproducibility information
Well-motivated problem addressing neural network strategy representation in large-scale games where averaging is expensive
Clear presentation with good intuitive explanations (e.g., Figure 2 landscape analysis) and honest discussion of limitations including anchoring mechanism solution

Asymmetric approach requires solving problem twice to compute both equilibrium components, eliminating practical advantage over symmetric methods and requiring clear specification of which player to perturb

Limited experimental scope: normal-form games are synthetic/small-scale, extensive-form games are standard benchmarks, and no experiments on stated motivation of large-scale games with neural networks

strengths: Novel asymmetric perturbation insight: simple idea with strong theoretical justification that equilibrium strategies coincide exactly (not O(μ) approximation) for sufficiently small μ in an invariance regime

Sound theoretical contributions: Theorem 3.1 on equilibrium invariance is significant; Theorem 4.1 achieves linear last-iterate convergence despite asymmetric strong convexity; creative proof using piecewise affinity and Hoffman's bound handles projections carefully
Improved convergence rate: Linear rate provably faster than Õ(1/t) of symmetric perturbation (Liu et al. 2023); parameter-free variant requires only O(ln(1/ε)) episodes
Impossibility result strengthens contribution: Theorem B.1 formally proves symmetric perturbation almost never reaches original equilibrium, supporting motivation
Well-structured presentation with clear intuition (Figure 2), extensive proofs, and honest discussion of limitations; experiments on both normal-form and extensive-form games
weaknesses: Theory restricted to bilinear games: Near-linearity structure g(x)=max_y x^T Ay is essential to proof; extensions to convex-concave or other settings unclear despite abstract mentioning large-scale games with neural networks

Game-dependent constant α not computable: Theorem 3.1 requires μ < α/max||x||, but α is defined implicitly via Lemma E.1 with no explicit formula or practical estimation algorithm provided; practitioners lack principled way to determine invariance regime a priori

Gap between theory and extensive-form experiments: Analysis covers L₂ perturbation, but Section 5 uses dilated Euclidean regularizer for sequence-form games without rigorously justifying that invariance and convergence extend to this setting

Limited experimental scope relative to claims: Normal-form experiments on small strategy spaces (2-5 dimensions); abstract promises large-scale games with neural network policies but none are tested; no timing comparisons or large-scale validation

Practical applicability concerns: Parameter-free procedure still requires initialization μ_init choice affecting convergence speed; learning rate constraint η ≤ μ/(μ²+||A||²) adds tuning burden; alternating update requirement (recent, from Lee et al. 2024) limits generality
